proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(s\in\mathbb R^{\Omega}\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), and let
\[
R=\{x\in\Omega:p_K(x;s)\leq\alpha\}.
\]
If \(R=\varnothing\), then \(\Pr_{\pi}\{X\in R\}=0\leq\alpha\).  Otherwise, order
\(R\) as \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{|R|}\) so that
\(s(\sigma_1)\geq\cdots\geq s(\sigma_{|R|})\), breaking ties arbitrarily.  For
\(P_j=\{\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_j\}\), the ordering implies
\[
P_j\subseteq\{y\in\Omega:s(y)\geq s(\sigma_j)\}.
\]
Nonnegativity of the entries of \(K\), its row-stochasticity in
\(\texttt{ass:row-stochastic}\), and \(\texttt{def:kernel-tail-value}\) therefore give
\[
K(\sigma_j,P_j)
 \leq K\bigl(\sigma_j,\{y:s(y)\geq s(\sigma_j)\}\bigr)
 =p_K(\sigma_j;s)\leq\alpha.
\]
Taking the maximum over \(j\) and then using the minimum in
\(\texttt{def:subset-degeneracy}\) yields \(d_K(R)\leq\alpha\).  If all subset
inequalities hold, then
\[
\Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{p_K(X;s)\leq\alpha\}=\pi(R)\leq d_K(R)\leq\alpha,
\]
which is universal validity as defined in \(\texttt{def:universal-validity}\).

Conversely, suppose that \(d_K(A)<\pi(A)\) for a nonempty \(A\).  Finiteness of
\(\operatorname{Ord}(A)\) gives an ordering \(\sigma\) attaining the minimum in
\(d_K(A)\).  Choose a strictly decreasing score along this ordering,
\(s(\sigma_1)>\cdots>s(\sigma_{|A|})\), and give every point of
\(\Omega\setminus A\) a score strictly below \(s(\sigma_{|A|})\).  Then the upper
score set of \(\sigma_j\) is exactly \(P_j\), whence
\[
p_K(\sigma_j;s)=K(\sigma_j,P_j)\leq d_K(A),\qquad 1\leq j\leq |A|.
\]
At the admissible threshold \(\alpha=d_K(A)\), the rejection set contains \(A\),
and hence has design probability at least \(\pi(A)>\alpha\).  This contradicts
universal validity and proves necessity.  Notice that the weak rejection inequality
causes no boundary gap: equality \(p_K=\alpha\) is included on both sides.

The condition is necessary on the full row-kernel class, not merely on partition
kernels.  It also admits nonpartition kernels.  Indeed, for uniform \(\pi\) on
three points, the cyclic matrix with diagonal entries \(2/3\), entries \(1/3\) on
the directed cycle, and all other entries zero has singleton degeneracy \(2/3\),
two-point degeneracy \(2/3\), and full-set degeneracy \(1\).  These are at least
the corresponding masses \(1/3,2/3,1\), so the equivalence just proved makes it
valid.  Its three two-point row supports overlap without coinciding, whereas rows
arising by conditioning \(\pi\) on partition cells either have disjoint supports
or are identical.  Thus it is not a partition kernel.

Set \(d_K(\varnothing)=0\) as in \(\texttt{def:subset-degeneracy}\).  For nonempty
\(A\), partition the finite set \(\operatorname{Ord}(A)\) according to the last
element \(i\).  If \(\sigma_{|A|}=i\), the last prefix is \(A\), so the last
contribution to the ordering maximum is \(K(i,A)\).  The preceding entries form an
arbitrary ordering \(\rho\) of \(A\setminus\{i\}\), and their smallest achievable
maximum is \(d_K(A\setminus\{i\})\).  Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_K(A)
&=\min_{i\in A}\min_{\rho\in\operatorname{Ord}(A\setminus\{i\})}
  \max\left\{K(i,A),\max_{1\leq j\leq |A|-1}
  K(\rho_j,P_j(\rho))\right\}\\
&=\min_{i\in A}\max\{K(i,A),d_K(A\setminus\{i\})\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses the elementary identity
\(\min_{\rho}\max\{a,g(\rho)\}=\max\{a,\min_{\rho}g(\rho)\}\), valid because the
minimum is over a finite set.

For the operation count, first compute every row subset sum \(K(i,A)\) by the
recursion \(K(i,A)=K(i,A\setminus\{j\})+K(i,j)\).  This takes
\(O(m2^m)\) additions.  Evaluating the displayed recursion for every subset then
requires
\[
\sum_{A\subseteq\Omega}|A|=m2^{m-1}
\]
candidate evaluations, hence \(O(m2^m)\) arithmetic operations in total.  Store,
for every nonempty \(A\), a minimizing last element \(i_A\).  Recursively following
\(A,A\setminus\{i_A\},\ldots\) and reversing the stored deletion sequence produces
an ordering attaining \(d_K(A)\).  Consequently, after comparing the computed
values with the known masses \(\pi(A)\), any subset with
\(d_K(A)<\pi(A)\), together with its recovered ordering, is an exact violated-subset
certificate.

We first prove the equivalence of the degeneracy and core conditions.  Suppose that
\(C\subseteq A\) is nonempty and satisfies \(K(i,C)\geq t\) for every \(i\in C\).
For an arbitrary ordering \(\sigma\) of \(A\), let \(\sigma_j\) be the last member
of \(C\) to occur.  Then \(C\subseteq P_j(\sigma)\), and nonnegativity of \(K\)
gives
\[
K(\sigma_j,P_j(\sigma))\geq K(\sigma_j,C)\geq t.
\]
Thus every ordering maximum is at least \(t\), so \(d_K(A)\geq t\).

For the converse, assume a peeling run deletes all points, in deletion order
\(i_1,\ldots,i_{|A|}\).  Immediately before deleting \(i_j\), the current set is
\(B_j=\{i_j,\ldots,i_{|A|}\}\) and
\(K(i_j,B_j)<t\).  The reverse ordering
\(\sigma=(i_{|A|},\ldots,i_1)\) has \(B_j\) as the prefix ending at \(i_j\).
Consequently every prefix mass in this ordering is strictly below \(t\), and
\(d_K(A)<t\).  Contrapositively, \(d_K(A)\geq t\) prevents complete deletion.

The conclusion is independent of deletion choices.  If a core \(C\) exists and
the current set \(B\) contains \(C\), then for each \(i\in C\),
\(K(i,B)\geq K(i,C)\geq t\); hence no member of \(C\) can be deleted.  Conversely,
any nonempty terminal set produced by the procedure satisfies the defining core
inequalities.  Thus the procedure leaves a nonempty set if and only if a core
exists, and the preceding two paragraphs establish all three equivalences.  Taking
\(t=\pi(A)\) and invoking \(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\) gives the final
universal-validity assertion.  Positivity in
\(\texttt{ass:positive-finite-design}\) also shows at the singleton boundary that
\(K(i,i)\geq\pi(i)>0\) is necessary.

By \(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\) and
\(\texttt{def:subset-degeneracy}\), validity is equivalent, for every nonempty
\(A\), to
\[
\min_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Ord}(A)}
\max_{1\leq j\leq |A|}K(\sigma_j,P_j(\sigma))\geq\pi(A).
\]
A minimum of finitely many quantities is at least \(\pi(A)\) exactly when each is,
and a finite maximum is at least \(\pi(A)\) exactly when at least one constituent
is.  Hence the condition is exactly
\[
\bigcap_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Ord}(A)}
\bigcup_{j=1}^{|A|}
\{K:K(\sigma_j,P_j(\sigma))\geq\pi(A)\}.
\]
Intersecting this expression over nonempty \(A\) and with
\(\mathcal K_L\) proves the displayed description in the statement.  Each set in
braces is a closed half-space, while \(\mathcal K_L\) is defined by finitely many
linear equalities and inequalities under \(\texttt{ass:row-stochastic}\) and
\(\texttt{ass:legal-support}\).  Distributing the finitely many intersections over
the finitely many unions therefore gives an exact finite union of closed
polyhedra.

For an explicit core mixed-integer representation, for each nonempty \(A\) introduce
\(z_{A i}\in\{0,1\}\) for \(i\in A\), require
\(\sum_{i\in A}z_{A i}\geq1\), and introduce continuous variables
\(v_{Aij}\) for \(i,j\in A\).  The linear constraints
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\leq v_{Aij}\leq K(i,j),\qquad v_{Aij}\leq z_{Aj},\qquad
v_{Aij}\geq K(i,j)+z_{Aj}-1,\\
\sum_{j\in A}v_{Aij}\geq \pi(A)z_{Ai}\qquad(i\in A)
\end{gathered}
\]
force \(v_{Aij}=z_{Aj}K(i,j)\), because \(0\leq K(i,j)\leq1\).  Thus the selected
set \(C_A=\{i:z_{Ai}=1\}\) is nonempty and every selected row obeys
\(K(i,C_A)\geq\pi(A)\).  Conversely any core supplies feasible \(z,v\).  The
equivalence in \(\texttt{thm:peeling-core}\) proves exactness.  Finally,
\(\texttt{thm:subset-recursion}\) computes a violated \(A\) and an attaining
ordering whenever one exists, so it is an exact finite separator.

Let \(K\in\mathcal P_L\) arise from a partition \(\mathcal G\).  Positivity of
\(\pi\) makes \(\pi(G)>0\) for every nonempty cell.  Fix nonempty \(A\) and an
arbitrary ordering \(\sigma\) of \(A\).  For each cell \(G\) meeting \(A\), consider
the last element \(i_G\) of \(A\cap G\) in this ordering.  Its prefix contains
\(A\cap G\), so
\[
K(i_G,P(i_G))\geq \frac{\pi(A\cap G)}{\pi(G)}.
\]
Writing \(r_G=\pi(A\cap G)/\pi(G)\), we have
\[
\pi(A)=\sum_{G\in\mathcal G}\pi(G)r_G
\leq \max_{G\in\mathcal G}r_G,
\]
because the cell masses sum to one.  Hence every ordering has a prefix mass at
least \(\pi(A)\), so \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\).  The characterization in
\(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\) proves universal validity.

For strictness, take uniform \(\pi\), complete \(L\), and the displayed cyclic
matrix.  Row sums are one and all entries are legal.  For a singleton,
\(d_K(\{i\})=K(i,i)=2/3\).  For every two-point set, one of its two orderings has
maximum prefix mass \(2/3\), and the first prefix in either ordering has mass
\(2/3\), so its degeneracy is exactly \(2/3\).  For \(A=\Omega\), the last prefix
has row mass one in every ordering, so \(d_K(\Omega)=1\).  These values dominate
\(1/3,2/3,1\), respectively, proving validity.  If it were a partition kernel, the
positive entry \(K(1,2)\) would put \(1,2\) in one cell, \(K(2,3)>0\) would put
\(2,3\) in one cell, and hence all three points would share a cell.  Conditioning
uniform \(\pi\) on that cell would give every row \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\), contrary to
the displayed matrix.  Thus the inclusion is strict.

Write
\[
a_{hxy}=\mathbf 1\{s^h(y)\geq s^h(x)\},\qquad
q_{hx}(K)=\sum_{y\in\Omega}a_{hxy}K(x,y).
\]
These coefficients are fixed by \(\texttt{ass:prespecified-catalogue}\), and
\(q_{hx}(K)=p_K(x;s^h)\).  Introduce a binary \(z_{hx}\) and impose
\[
q_{hx}(K)\leq \alpha+1-z_{hx}.
\]
If \(z_{hx}=1\), this is exactly the closed rejection condition
\(q_{hx}(K)\leq\alpha\); if \(z_{hx}=0\), it is vacuous because
\(0\leq q_{hx}(K)\leq1\).  Thus every feasible point satisfies
\(z_{hx}\leq\mathbf 1\{q_{hx}(K)\leq\alpha\}\), and for each fixed \(K\) equality
can be chosen.  Maximizing
\[
\sum_{h=1}^q w_h\sum_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x)z_{hx}
\]
therefore has optimal value exactly \(\max_K\operatorname{Pow}(K)\), including at
the boundary \(q_{hx}(K)=\alpha\).  Zero catalogue weights do not affect the
equality of optimal values; the returned rejection probability is evaluated from
the displayed closed condition.

It remains to encode validity.  For every nonempty \(A\), every
\(\sigma\in\operatorname{Ord}(A)\), and every \(j\), introduce
\(y_{A\sigma j}\in\{0,1\}\), and impose
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{|A|}y_{A\sigma j}\geq1,
\qquad
K(\sigma_j,P_j(\sigma))\geq
\pi(A)-(1-y_{A\sigma j}).
\]
When \(y_{A\sigma j}=0\), the second inequality is vacuous because
\(\pi(A)-1\leq0\); when it is one, it selects the required half-space.  By
\(\texttt{thm:polyhedral-description}\), these constraints, together with
\(0\leq K(x,y)\leq1\), row sums one, and the legal-support zero restrictions, are
an exact finite mixed-integer linear formulation of the program defining
\(K^\star\).

For termination and certification, solve a master formulation and, at any proposed
kernel, run the recursion in \(\texttt{thm:subset-recursion}\).  If it finds
\(d_K(A)<\pi(A)\), its stored ordering \(\sigma\) identifies one of the finitely
many omitted disjunctions above, which is then added.  No disjunction is added
twice, so this cutting phase is finite.  Branching is also finite because the full
formulation has finitely many binary variables.  At a leaf, feasibility is a finite
linear-inequality question.  Fourier--Motzkin elimination terminates after the
finite number of continuous variables: each elimination replaces the upper and
lower bounds for one variable by their finitely many pairwise consequences, which
preserves feasibility in both directions.  Its trace either reconstructs a feasible
point or ends in a contradictory constant inequality.  Thus exhaustive branching,
used as a fallback to any faster branch-and-cut implementation, returns either an
infeasibility certificate or a feasible incumbent together with elimination traces
excluding every branch having larger objective.  The latter finite collection is a
global upper-bound certificate.  The selected \(y\)'s record active validity
disjuncts, and direct evaluation of the \(z\)-conditions records exact rejection
probability.

Finally, the legal partition kernels are finite in number because \(\Omega\) has
finitely many partitions.  Each can be evaluated exactly.  Every such kernel is
valid by the same cell argument: for any \(A\), some cell has
\(\pi(A\cap G)/\pi(G)\geq\pi(A)\), and the last member of \(A\cap G\) in any
ordering has at least that prefix mass.  Hence their maximum power is no larger
than the unrestricted valid optimum.  In the feasible case, singleton validity and
positivity give \(K(i,i)\geq\pi(i)>0\), so legal support contains every self-loop;
the singleton partition is therefore a legal benchmark, and the partition maximum
is well defined.  Consequently
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{part}}
=\operatorname{Pow}(K^\star)-\max_{K\in\mathcal P_L}\operatorname{Pow}(K)\geq0.
\]
The two independently certified optimum values prove strict dominance over every
partition kernel whenever this difference is positive.  Outcome-freeness in
\(\texttt{ass:outcome-free-kernel}\) ensures that this optimization remains a
design-stage choice rather than an outcome-adaptive test.

The displayed matrix is row-stochastic and is supported on the stated directed
relation \(L\).  Its singleton degeneracies are all \(2/3\).  For a two-point
subset, each possible first prefix has mass \(2/3\), and direct inspection of the
two orderings shows that one ordering has maximum \(2/3\); hence every two-point
degeneracy is \(2/3\).  The last prefix for \(A=\Omega\) has mass one, so
\(d_K(\Omega)=1\).  Therefore
\[
d_K(A)\geq |A|/3=\pi(A)
\]
for every nonempty \(A\), and \(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\) certifies
validity.

Under \(s^1(1)>s^1(2)>s^1(3)\), the three upper-tail values are
\[
p_K(1;s^1)=K(1,\{1\})=\frac23,
\quad
p_K(2;s^1)=K(2,\{1,2\})=\frac23,
\quad
p_K(3;s^1)=K(3,\Omega)=1.
\]
Thus, at \(\alpha=2/3\), precisely states one and two reject, and
\(\operatorname{Pow}(K)=2/3\).  Universal validity itself supplies the matching
upper bound: for this fixed catalogue score, every feasible kernel has rejection
mass at most \(\alpha=2/3\).  Hence the displayed kernel is globally
catalogue-power optimal.

It remains to evaluate the partition benchmark.  If two distinct states shared a
partition cell, positivity of \(\pi\) would make both directed transitions between
them positive in the corresponding conditional kernel.  The stated \(L\) contains
only one direction for each unordered pair.  Thus every legal partition has only
singleton cells, its kernel is the identity, and every upper-tail value is one.
Its power is zero.  Therefore
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{part}}=2/3-0=2/3\), as claimed.

Let \(Y\) denote the true fixed schedule.  Under the bounded null in the theorem,
for every realized assignment \(x\), the schedule \(Y\) is consistent with the
outcomes observed at \(x\) and satisfies the effect-count restriction.  Hence
\(Y\in\Theta_{r,c}(x,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}(x))\).  Statistic imputability and fixed peer
exposure make the score vector
\[
s_Y(y)=T(y,Y_Y(y)),\qquad y\in\Omega,
\]
a well-defined deterministic vector once the fixed schedule is held fixed.  By the
definition of the supremum,
\[
p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(x)
\geq p_K(x;s_Y)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\Omega.
\]
The subset condition and \(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\) imply
\[
\Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{p_K(X;s_Y)\leq\alpha\}\leq\alpha.
\]
The pointwise inequality reverses the inclusion of lower-tail events:
\[
\{p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha\}
\subseteq\{p_K(X;s_Y)\leq\alpha\}.
\]
Taking design probabilities proves the result.  The fixed-potential-outcome and
outcome-free-kernel assumptions are essential here: they ensure that the same
deterministic score vector and kernel are used at every possible value of \(X\).

A nontrivial pairwise rank comparison uses outcomes of two distinct focal units,
so necessarily \(N\geq2\).  One assignment cannot give either unit own-treatment
variation.  If \(m=2\) and every focal unit varies between the only two states,
then for every \(u\) the two states use different coordinates
\(\theta_u(0,e)\) and \(\theta_u(1,e)\).  Thus no potential-outcome coordinate can
appear in both assignment scores, contrary to the stipulated shared-coordinate
property.  Hence \(m\geq3\).

The handle attains these bounds.  With treatment vectors \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\),
unit one varies on the legal comparison \(1\to2\), and unit two varies on
\(2\to3\) (and also on \(3\to1\)).  The three comparisons use, respectively,
\[
(\theta_1(0,e),\theta_2(0,e)),\qquad
(\theta_1(1,e),\theta_2(0,e)),\qquad
(\theta_1(0,e),\theta_2(1,e)).
\]
Thus \(\theta_2(0,e)\) is shared by the first two scores and
\(\theta_1(0,e)\) by the first and third.  Moreover, the null inequalities involve
the differences
\(\theta_1(1,e)-\theta_1(0,e)\) and
\(\theta_2(1,e)-\theta_2(0,e)\), so the resulting constraint graph is connected.
This hypergraph contains a genuine nonproduct instance.  For example, take the
realized assignment to be state \(2\) and take \(r=N\), so the effect-count
restriction is vacuous.  Consistency fixes \(\theta_1(1,e)\) and
\(\theta_2(0,e)\), while \(\theta_1(0,e)\) and \(\theta_2(1,e)\) remain free.  In
the product of the three assignment-wise marginal schedule sets, one could combine
a state-\(1\) component having one value of \(\theta_1(0,e)\) with a state-\(3\)
component having a different value, whereas every globally compatible schedule
enforces equality of those repeated coordinates.  Both marginal values are
individually feasible, so the globally compatible image is a proper subset of the
product.  This proves existence of a genuinely coupled minimal instance.  It also
shows why the unrestricted assertion for every observation and every null would be
too strong: if state \(1\) is observed and \(r=N\), both repeated baseline
coordinates are fixed constants and the remaining two coordinates separate.

No interference makes \(Y_u(1,e)-Y_u(0,e)\) the ordinary individual treatment
effect, and the elementary order-statistic equivalence
\[
\sum_{u\in U}\mathbf 1\{\tau_u(e)>c\}\leq r
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\tau_{(N-r)}(e)\leq c
\]
holds for \(r<N\), with the \(r=N\) null vacuous.  In both comparator designs, the
specified \(K\) is a partition kernel and is universally valid by
\(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\).  The pointwise schedule-supremum argument
in \(\texttt{thm:composite-null-validity}\) therefore makes the frozen worst-case
test an exact randomization test for its own assignment-specific score.  What fails
is the asserted equality with the cited adjusted-outcome tests.

Indeed, use one complete-randomization cell with two units and exactly one treated
unit.  Write \(x_i\) for the assignment treating unit \(i\), set
\(\pi(x_i)=1/2\), let \(K(x_i,x_j)=1/2\), and use \(\phi(r)=r\).  Consider the
no-interference schedule
\[
\theta_1(0,e)=1,\quad \theta_1(1,e)=3,
\qquad
\theta_2(0,e)=0,\quad \theta_2(1,e)=2,
\]
and suppose \(X=x_1\).  The observed vector is \((3,0)\).  The frozen score uses
the assignment-specific outcome vectors \((3,0)\) and \((1,2)\); in each, the
treated unit has ascending rank two.  Hence
\[
p_K(x_1;s_\theta)=\frac12\mathbf 1\{2\geq2\}
+\frac12\mathbf 1\{2\geq2\}=1.
\]
Both individual effects are exactly \(2\), so for \(r=0,c=2\) this schedule is
null-compatible and \(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}(x_1)=1\).

The Caughey adjusted-outcome construction at boundary \(2\) instead fixes
\((3,0)-2(1,0)=(1,0)\) while permuting treatment.  The treated rank is then two at
\(x_1\) and one at \(x_2\), giving upper-tail value \(1/2\).  The cited individual
and simultaneous conclusions in
\(\texttt{lem:caughey-quantile-specialization}\) concern this latter construction.
Thus the two tests are not identical.  The Su--Li class contains the same example
as its one-stratum case, so the claimed exact multiple-choice-knapsack reduction is
also not a specialization of the frozen score map, notwithstanding the published
result in \(\texttt{lem:suli-knapsack-specialization}\).  This explicit witness
proves the corrected negative statement.

theorem.statement:
The finite-computation and simultaneous-inference parts have a positive answer in
exact finite arithmetic.  Fix the realized assignment
\(x_0=X\).  For each subset \(Q\subseteq U\) with \(|Q|=N-r\), and for each family
of total weak orders \((\mathcal W_x:x\in\Omega)\) of the imputed focal outcomes,
consider the margin linear program in variables \(v_{ua}=\theta_u(a,e)\) and
\(0\leq\varepsilon\leq1\): impose observed-outcome consistency, impose
\(v_{u1}-v_{u0}\leq c\) for \(u\in Q\), impose equality within every tie block of
\(\mathcal W_x\), and impose a gap at least \(\varepsilon\) between consecutive
strict blocks after substituting \(Y_{\theta,u}(x)=v_{u,Z_u(x)}\).  A pattern is
feasible exactly when the maximum margin is positive.  On each feasible pattern
the fixed rank rule makes every \(s_{\theta}(x)\) constant, and
\[
p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(x_0)=
\max_{Q,(\mathcal W_x)}
\left\{
\sum_{y\in\Omega}K(x_0,y)
\mathbf 1\{s_{Q,\mathcal W}(y)\geq s_{Q,\mathcal W}(x_0)\}:
\text{the margin optimum is positive}
\right\}.
\]
The maximum is over a finite set, and an LP witness for a maximizing pattern extends
to an optimizing compatible sharp schedule.  Hence this is a terminating exact LP
enumeration, equivalently a finite disjunctive mixed-integer formulation, for every
\(r\) and \(c\).  For \(j=0,\ldots,N\), define
\[
\gamma_j(\alpha)=
\sup\{c\in\mathbb R:p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{N-j,c}(X)\leq\alpha\},
\qquad \sup\varnothing=-\infty.
\]
The inversion cutoff is finite-program computable as well.  For
\(j\geq1\), and for each pattern with \(|Q|=j\) whose kernel tail mass is greater
than \(\alpha\), let
\[
b_{Q,\mathcal W}=\inf\left\{
\max_{u\in Q}(v_{u1}-v_{u0}):
v\text{ is observed-consistent and realizes }(\mathcal W_x:x\in\Omega)
\right\}.
\]
Discard patterns having no positive-margin realization.  Then
\[
\gamma_j(\alpha)=
\min_{\substack{Q,(\mathcal W_x):\\
\text{tail mass}>\alpha}}b_{Q,\mathcal W},
\qquad \min\varnothing=+\infty.
\]
Each \(b_{Q,\mathcal W}\) is obtained by one linear program after the
positive-margin feasibility check, by introducing
\(h\geq v_{u1}-v_{u0}\) for \(u\in Q\) and minimizing \(h\) over the closure of
the weak-order cell.

Then \(\gamma_0(\alpha)\leq\cdots\leq\gamma_N(\alpha)\).  If
\(\gamma_N(\alpha)=+\infty\), then \(\mathcal C_{\alpha}=\varnothing\) and every
\(\ell_k(e;\alpha)=+\infty\).  Otherwise \(\mathcal C_{\alpha}\neq\varnothing\)
and the exact projection identity has the computable form
\[
\ell_k(e;\alpha)
=\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal C_{\alpha}}\theta_{(k)}(e)
=\gamma_k(\alpha),\qquad k=1,\ldots,N.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\Pr_{X\sim\pi}\{\tau_{(k)}(e)\geq\ell_k(e;\alpha)
\text{ for every }k=1,\ldots,N\}\geq1-\alpha.
\]
The requested conjunction nevertheless has a negative comparator clause under the
frozen schedule-score definition.  Even in one two-unit complete-randomization cell,
the assignment-specific score \(T(x,Y_\theta(x))\) need not equal the adjusted-outcome
score used by the Caughey--Dafoe--Li--Miratrix reduction; the one-stratum Su--Li
clause inherits the same obstruction.  For the three-assignment, two-unit coupled
pattern the enumeration consists of finitely many LPs over the four shared coordinates
\(\theta_1(0,e),\theta_1(1,e),\theta_2(0,e),\theta_2(1,e)\), so it solves that
nonproduct instance without relaxing the shared-coordinate equalities.
theorem.proof_tex:
Write \(v_{ua}=\theta_u(a,e)\).  By fixed peer exposure, assignment \(x\) uses the
coordinate \(v_{u,Z_u(x)}\) for focal unit \(u\).  Consistency with the realized
data is therefore the finite linear system
\[
v_{u,Z_u(x_0)}=Y_u^{\mathrm{obs}},\qquad u\in U.
\]
The count restriction has an exact closed disjunctive representation:
\[
\sum_{u\in U}\mathbf 1\{v_{u1}-v_{u0}>c\}\leq r
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists Q\subseteq U,\ |Q|=N-r,\quad
v_{u1}-v_{u0}\leq c\ \text{for every }u\in Q.
\]
For the forward implication choose \(N-r\) nonexceeding units; the reverse
implication leaves at most the \(r\) units outside \(Q\) able to exceed.  This
representation is why no artificial bound or big-\(M\) constant is needed for the
strict effect indicator.

For each assignment, a total weak order is an ordered partition of the finite set
\(U\).  Within a block impose equality of the corresponding coordinates
\(v_{u,Z_u(x)}\); between consecutive blocks impose that every value in the upper
block minus every value in the lower block is at least \(\varepsilon\).  Together
with the consistency and null inequalities, these are linear constraints.  If a
specified weak order is realized by some schedule, the finitely many strict gaps
have a positive minimum, so the margin program is feasible with some
\(\varepsilon>0\).  Conversely, a solution with positive margin realizes exactly
that weak order.  Maximizing \(\varepsilon\) subject also to
\(0\leq\varepsilon\leq1\) therefore decides the cell exactly; equality patterns
are not lost and strict patterns cannot be accepted at zero margin.

There are finitely many choices of \(Q\) and finitely many total weak orders on
\(U\), hence finitely many families indexed by \(\Omega\).  Because \(T\) is a
fixed rank statistic with a deterministic tie rule, its value on each assignment
depends only on the selected weak order.  Thus the entire score vector, and hence
the kernel tail mass at \(x_0\), is constant on a cell.  Every compatible schedule
lies in at least one enumerated \(Q\)-disjunct and exactly one weak-order family;
every positive-margin LP witness is a compatible schedule.  Maximizing the finitely
many resulting constants proves the displayed formula and attainment.  Potential
outcomes at exposure levels not used in the fiber do not enter any constraint or
score and may be filled arbitrarily, giving a full schedule \(\theta\).  In the
minimal coupled handle there are only three assignment weak orders on two units
and four shared \(v\)-coordinates, so the same construction directly solves the
advertised instance while retaining both repeated-coordinate equalities.

For completeness, fix \(j\geq1\), put \(r=N-j\), and consider a pattern having
tail mass strictly greater than \(\alpha\).  It is feasible at threshold \(c\)
exactly when it has a realization with
\(\max_{u\in Q}(v_{u1}-v_{u0})\leq c\).  Its feasibility threshold is therefore
\(b_{Q,\mathcal W}\).  Once a positive-margin realization exists, the infimum over
the relatively open weak-order cell equals the minimum over its closure: if
\(\bar v\) is in the closure and \(v^\circ\) is one positive-margin realization,
then \((1-\lambda)\bar v+\lambda v^\circ\) realizes the strict order for every
\(\lambda>0\), respects all closed consistency constraints, and approaches
\(\bar v\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\).  The closure program is linear after adding
\(h\geq v_{u1}-v_{u0}\) and minimizing \(h\).  Endpoint attainment can be checked
by the positive-margin LP at \(c=b_{Q,\mathcal W}\), but it does not affect the
supremum cutoff.  The worst-case value is at most \(\alpha\) precisely while no
pattern of tail mass greater than \(\alpha\) is feasible.  Taking the first
feasibility threshold over the finite catalogue proves
\[
\gamma_j(\alpha)=\min_{\text{tail mass}>\alpha}b_{Q,\mathcal W}.
\]
If the catalogue in this minimum is empty, the worst-case value is at most
\(\alpha\) for every \(c\), and both sides have the stipulated value \(+\infty\).
For \(j=0\), the null is independent of \(c\), so \(\gamma_0\) is obtained by one
run of the same finite enumeration and is either \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\).

We next prove the projection formula.  Let
\(n_c(\theta)=\sum_u\mathbf 1\{\theta_u(1,e)-\theta_u(0,e)>c\}\).  For
\(j=N-r\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), elementary order-statistic algebra gives
\[
n_c(\theta)>r\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\theta_{(j)}(e)>c.
\]
For \(r=N\), the left side is impossible.  Also,
\(\Theta_{r,c}\subseteq\Theta_{r',c'}\) whenever \(r\leq r'\) and \(c\leq c'\).
Taking suprema shows that \(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}\) is nondecreasing in each of
\(r,c\).  It follows that every rejected-threshold set is a lower subset of
\(\mathbb R\), and that
\(\gamma_0\leq\cdots\leq\gamma_N\).

Using the displayed order-statistic equivalence in
\(\texttt{def:joint-confidence-region}\), the region is exactly the set of
schedules satisfying
\[
\theta_{(j)}(e)>c
\quad\text{for every }j=0,\ldots,N
\text{ and every }c\text{ with }
p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{N-j,c}(X)\leq\alpha,
\]
where the \(j=0\) requirement is impossible whenever it occurs.  If
\(\gamma_N=+\infty\), some order-statistic coordinate is required to exceed an
unbounded sequence, so the region is empty.  If \(\gamma_N<+\infty\), all cutoffs
are finite above.  The monotone sequence of cutoffs permits a nondecreasing effect
vector whose \(j\)-th coordinate is strictly above every rejected \(c\) for that
\(j\); arbitrary baselines then realize it as a schedule.  Thus the region is
nonempty.  Every member has \(\theta_{(k)}(e)\geq\gamma_k\).  Conversely, for each
\(\eta>0\), choose its first \(k\) ordered effects above their respective rejected
sets but with the \(k\)-th no larger than \(\gamma_k+\eta\), and choose later
effects sufficiently large to clear their finite cutoffs.  This proves
\(\inf_{\mathcal C_\alpha}\theta_{(k)}(e)=\gamma_k\), including the case
\(\gamma_k=-\infty\) by sending the first \(k\) effects to minus infinity.

For simultaneous coverage, let \(Y\) be the true schedule and let \(s_Y\) be its
fixed imputed score vector.  If \(Y\notin\mathcal C_\alpha\), there are \(r,c\) such
that the true schedule satisfies \(n_c(Y)\leq r\) while
\(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha\).  At every assignment the true schedule is
one of the schedules in that supremum, so
\[
p_K(X;s_Y)\leq p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{r,c}(X)\leq\alpha.
\]
Thus the union over all true bounded nulls is contained in the single event
\(\{p_K(X;s_Y)\leq\alpha\}\).  By
\(\texttt{thm:universal-validity-iff}\), the latter has probability at most
\(\alpha\).  On \(Y\in\mathcal C_\alpha\), every true ordered effect is at least
the corresponding projection infimum, proving the simultaneous statement without
a multiplicity penalty.

It remains to test the demanded comparator identity.  Take \(N=2\), let
\(\Omega=\{x_1,x_2\}\) be complete randomization of exactly one treated unit, with
\(x_i\) treating unit \(i\), let \(\pi(x_i)=1/2\), and let every row of \(K\) equal
\(\pi\).  Use \(\phi(r)=r\), and consider the no-interference schedule
\[
\theta_1(0,e)=1,\quad \theta_1(1,e)=3,
\qquad
\theta_2(0,e)=0,\quad \theta_2(1,e)=2.
\]
At the realized assignment \(X=x_1\), the observed outcome vector is \((3,0)\).
For the frozen assignment-specific schedule score, the treated unit has rank two
under both assignments: the imputed vectors are \((3,0)\) at \(x_1\) and
\((1,2)\) at \(x_2\).  Hence
\[
s_\theta(x_1)=s_\theta(x_2)=2,
\qquad p_K(x_1;s_\theta)=1.
\]
Both effects equal \(2\), so the schedule belongs to \(\Theta_{0,2}\), and in fact
\(p^{\mathrm{wc}}_{0,2}(x_1)=1\).

In contrast, the adjusted-outcome vector at the sharp boundary \(2\) is
\((3,0)-2(1,0)=(1,0)\).  Holding this vector fixed while permuting the one treated
label gives rank score two at \(x_1\) and rank score one at \(x_2\), hence upper-tail
value \(1/2\).  This is the adjusted-outcome score construction underlying
\(\texttt{lem:caughey-quantile-specialization}\), not the assignment-specific map
in \(\texttt{def:schedule-score}\).  The claimed equality therefore fails already
for a legal, universally valid partition kernel.  Taking a single stratum makes the
same example a Su--Li design, so it also refutes the second claimed recovery.  Thus
the LP reduction, coupled-instance solution, projection identity, and simultaneous
coverage are proved, but exact recovery of those two published reductions requires
a different, assignment-invariant adjusted-outcome score definition and is false
under the frozen construction.

added_lemmas.statement:
Under an exchangeable complete-randomization law with a fixed treatment count and
a nondecreasing full-sample rank-score statistic, the bounded-null randomization
test yields an exact \(1-\alpha\) confidence set for each fixed ordered individual
effect \(\tau_{(k)}(e)\); the confidence-set construction obtained by inverting all
quantile nulls is simultaneously valid for all \(k\).

attestation.note: Checked against the publisher's article at the stated theorem and section; a stable DOI is supplied in place of a verbatim transcription.

added_lemmas.statement:
Under a product of independent within-stratum exchangeable complete-randomization
laws with fixed treated counts and a nondecreasing stratified rank-score statistic,
the exact bounded-quantile-null optimization reduces to a multiple-choice-knapsack
problem, and inversion of these tests gives simultaneous randomization-based
confidence sets for all ordered individual effects.

attestation.note: Checked against the publisher record and the authors' arXiv version at the stated sections; a stable DOI is supplied in place of a verbatim transcription.

Suppose \(K\) is row-stochastic and satisfies \(d_K(A)\geq\pi(A)\) for every
nonempty \(A\subseteq\Omega\).  The coupled-pattern handle is cardinality-minimal
among schedule problems having a nontrivial pairwise rank comparison,
own-treatment variation for every focal unit, and at least one potential-outcome
coordinate shared by two distinct assignment scores: necessarily \(N\geq2\) and
\(m\geq3\), and the handle attains \(N=2\) and \(m=3\).  Its repeated-coordinate
and effect-exceedance constraint hypergraph connects all three assignment-specific
rank comparisons.  It contains a genuine nonproduct compatible-schedule instance:
when state \(2\) is observed and \(r=N\), the common
\(\theta_1(0,e)\) coordinate couples the first and third scores.  This is an
existential structural certificate; it does not assert nonproductness for every
realized assignment and every effect-count null.
